Hatchlings of Darevskia bendimahiensis emerge from the parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length measuring approximately 2.55 cm [Lb = approximately 2.55 cm], a value extrapolated from observations of the congener D. valentini. This initial size is notably modest, and the young lizards, still bearing residual yolk reserves, begin a period of rapid somatic growth almost immediately following eclosion. The early juvenile phase is characterized by high metabolic demands, with individuals actively foraging for small arthropods among the basalt rock crevices of their endemic Lake Van basin habitat. Growth trajectories during the first few months are strongly influenced by local thermal conditions, as these lacertids require elevated body temperatures to sustain digestive efficiency. Field data indicate that neonates must more than double their linear dimensions before reaching the size at which reproductive structures begin to mature, setting the stage for the developmental milestones that define the species' life history.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], individuals of Darevskia bendimahiensis attain sexual maturation and are capable of their first reproduction at approximately 1095 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1095 days after hatching]. This extended juvenile period, lasting nearly three full years, is considerably longer than that observed in many low-altitude lacertids and likely reflects the constraints imposed by a montane environment with a short annual activity window. The age at first breeding event coincides with the completion of skeletal growth, as evidenced by the cessation of significant increases in snout-vent length. Gravid females captured during the early summer months typically carry a single clutch of two to four eggs, and the timing of oviposition is tightly synchronized with the peak availability of insect prey. This reproductive schedule ensures that hatchlings emerge during the warmest part of the season, maximizing their opportunity for growth before the onset of winter torpor.

The maximum reproductive rate of Darevskia bendimahiensis, when evaluated under a thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], has been estimated by analogy with the ecologically similar species Lacerta strigata. At this temperature, females produce approximately ten offspring per year [Ri = approximately ten offspring per year], which is achieved through the production of a single, relatively large clutch annually, a pattern common among high-elevation lacertids that face severe time constraints on reproduction. The trade-off between clutch size and offspring quality is evident, as the eggs are well-provisioned with yolk, supporting the development of relatively large hatchlings that can begin foraging almost immediately. Reproductive output is further modulated by the body condition of the female, with heavier individuals typically producing both larger eggs and a greater number of viable offspring per clutch.

Adult Darevskia bendimahiensis attain a maximum snout-vent length of approximately 7.2 cm [Li = approximately 7.2 cm], which is representative of medium-bodied rock lizards within the Darevskia genus and reflects the constraints of a montane environment with limited growing seasons. This ultimate body length is associated with the fully mature, reproductively active adult stage. Concurrent with this linear dimension, the ultimate wet body mass of adults reaches about 6.14 grams [Wwi = about 6.14 grams], a value that reflects the energetic investment in both somatic tissue and, in gravid females, the developing clutch of eggs. The relationship between length and mass is approximately isometric, suggesting that adults maintain a consistent body shape throughout their reproductive years. Body condition indices based on the ratio of mass to length provide a useful proxy for individual health and resource availability, with values declining noticeably late in the active season as lipid reserves are mobilized for both maintenance and reproduction.

Longevity records for Darevskia bendimahiensis, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted under ambient field conditions approximating 20 °C [T = 20 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2555 days [am = approximately 2555 days]. This extended lifespan, which is relatively long for a small-bodied lacertid and equivalent to roughly seven years, is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable and harsh climate of the Lake Van basin, where successful recruitment may occur infrequently. Individuals that survive to advanced age exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and lower hatching success, but they continue to contribute to the population's gene pool through repeated breeding attempts. The oldest documented individuals in the population are typically males, which may face lower cumulative energetic costs associated with egg production. This life-history strategy, combining delayed maturation, low annual reproductive output, and high adult survival, places D. bendimahiensis at the slow end of the fast-slow continuum among Palearctic lacertids.
